name: Central African Kanda
description: Kanda, meatballs simmered in tomato sauce, is a beloved dish from the Central African Republic - real technique uses toasted, ground pumpkin seeds in place of breadcrumbs as the meatball binder, which genuinely defines the dish; the raw meatballs go directly into the simmering sauce rather than being pre-cooked, which is what keeps them so tender.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Seeds, pumpkin and squash seed kernels, roasted, without salt

ingredients_full.note: tbsp, chopped, standing in for parsley

ingredients.ingredient: Seeds, pumpkin and squash seed kernels, roasted, without salt

steps_detailed: Mix the beef with the ground pumpkin seeds, garlic, and half the onion, kneading well until it forms a cohesive dough.
Shape into golf-ball-sized meatballs and refrigerate while you make the sauce.
Cook the remaining onion in a little oil, 3-4 minutes, then add the tomatoes and jalapeño, and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Carefully add the raw meatballs directly into the simmering sauce and cook 15-18 minutes, without stirring too much, until cooked through and tender.
Stir in the cilantro just before serving.

name: Central African Kanda ti Nyma
description: Kanda ti nyma, a groundnut-and-meat stew, is a genuinely different dish from the pumpkin-seed kanda despite the shared name - real versions build the dish on okra and real ground peanuts together, giving it a distinct, thicker, nuttier character.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef with the onion, 8-9 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter with the tomatoes and a little water, add to the pot.
Add the okra and simmer 20-22 minutes until the beef is tender and the stew has thickened naturally from the okra.

name: Central African Gozo
description: Gozo, a fermented cassava paste, is the foundational staple of Central African cuisine, served with nearly every meal - real technique lets the cassava flour ferment before cooking, which is what gives gozo its distinctive tang, and it's used to scoop up okra, peanut, or palm nut sauces.
steps_detailed: Mix the grated cassava with water and let ferment at room temperature 24 hours.
Cook the fermented mixture over medium heat, stirring constantly, 15-18 minutes, until thick and smooth.
steps: Mix the grated cassava with water and let ferment at room temperature 24 hours.

name: Central African Fufu
description: Fufu, pounded cassava, is another essential Central African staple, eaten like bread alongside stews and soups.
steps_detailed: Boil the cassava until completely soft, 20-25 minutes.
Drain and pound vigorously until smooth and stretchy, free of lumps.
steps: Boil the cassava until completely soft, 20-25 minutes.
Drain and pound vigorously until smooth and stretchy, free of lumps.

name: Central African Foutou
description: Foutou, pounded plantains (sometimes with mashed yam), is a genuine Central African staple, real technique boiling until completely soft before pounding.
steps_detailed: Boil the plantain until completely soft, 20-22 minutes.
Drain and pound vigorously until smooth and stretchy.
steps: Boil the plantain until completely soft, 20-22 minutes.

name: Central African Egusi Soup
description: Egusi soup, thickened with real ground melon seeds, is found throughout much of West and Central Africa, including the Central African Republic.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef, 6-7 minutes.
Mix the egusi with water into a paste and fry in spoonfuls in the palm oil, 5-6 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and beef, and simmer 10-12 minutes.
Stir in the spinach in the last 3 minutes.

name: Central African Muamba Chicken
description: Muamba, chicken with okra in a real palm oil and peanut sauce, shares its roots with the wider Central African moambe tradition found in both Congos and Angola.
steps_detailed: Brown the chicken in the palm oil, 8-9 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter with the tomatoes and a little water, add to the pot.
Add the okra and simmer 20-22 minutes until the chicken is tender.

name: Central African Bouillie
description: Bouillie, a warm porridge made from millet, rice, or cornmeal cooked with milk and sweetened with sugar, is a common Central African breakfast - real versions keep this simple, without more elaborate additions I can't specifically confirm as traditional.
steps_detailed: Blend the cooked rice with the milk until smooth.
Warm gently and stir in the sugar before serving.
steps: Blend the cooked rice with the milk until smooth.
Warm gently and stir in the sugar before serving.

name: Central African Grilled Fish
description: Grilled fish rubbed with garlic and ginger, reflecting the Central African Republic's Ubangi River fishing tradition.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and ginger, and let sit 10 minutes.
Grill or broil, 4-5 minutes per side, until just cooked through.

name: Central African Fried Plantain
description: Fried ripe plantain, a common side dish, real versions using genuinely ripe plantain for real caramelization.
steps_detailed: Fry the plantain slices in a little oil, turning once, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply caramelized and golden.

description: A simple, hearty beef and vegetable stew, common home cooking across the Central African Republic.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef with the onion, 8-9 minutes.
Add the carrot, potato, and tomatoes, and simmer 30-35 minutes until tender.

name: Central African Peanut Sauce
description: A simple ground-peanut sauce base, used across many stews in the Central African Republic.
steps_detailed: Whisk the peanut butter slowly with 1 cup water and the tomatoes into a smooth sauce.
Simmer 12-15 minutes until thickened.
